lessons.title: What a database actually is
objectives: Explain what a DBMS does that a flat file can't
Name the two broad DB families
Explain how DBMS changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect DBMS with durability and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A database is software that stores data durably and lets many programs read/write it safely at once, with guarantees a plain file can't give you: concurrent access without corruption, crash recovery, and fast lookups even at huge scale.
examples:
# Without a DBMS: two processes writing to the same file
# can corrupt it, or clobber each other's writes.
# A DBMS enforces safe concurrent access + durability guarantees.
commonMistakes: Assuming a database is 'just a fancy Excel file' — the concurrency and crash-safety guarantees are the whole point, not the storage format.
lessons.careerRelevance: Every backend service you'll build touches a database directly; this is foundational, not optional.

lessons.title: Primary & foreign keys
objectives: Define primary key and foreign key
Explain what a foreign key enforces
Explain how primary key changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect primary key with foreign key and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table (often an auto-incrementing id). A foreign key is a column in one table that references a primary key in another, and the database ENFORCES that the referenced row must exist — this is called referential integrity.
commonMistakes: Deleting a parent row (a customer) while orders still reference it — most databases block this by default unless you explicitly cascade or nullify.
lessons.careerRelevance: Schema design questions ('design a database for X') are a standard SWE interview format.
lessons.explain: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table (often an auto-incrementing id). A foreign key is a column in one table that references a primary key in another, and the database ENFORCES that the referenced row must exist — this is called referential integrity.

lessons.title: Data types & constraints
objectives: Pick appropriate column types
Use NOT NULL / UNIQUE / CHECK constraints
Explain how data types changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect data types with NOT NULL and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Choosing the right data type (INTEGER, TEXT, NUMERIC, BOOLEAN, TIMESTAMP) isn't just style — it affects storage size, valid values, and what operations are even possible. Constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK) let the database itself reject bad data, instead of relying on application code to catch every case.
commonMistakes: Storing dates/money as raw TEXT — you lose sorting, range queries, and arithmetic; use proper TIMESTAMP/NUMERIC types.
lessons.careerRelevance: Bad constraints are a leading cause of production data-integrity bugs — cheap to prevent, expensive to clean up later.

lessons.title: Normalization (1NF–3NF)
objectives: Explain what each normal form eliminates
Spot an un-normalized table
Explain how 1NF changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect 1NF with 2NF and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Normalization is the process of structuring tables to eliminate redundant data. 1NF: every cell holds one atomic value (no comma-separated lists in a column).
examples:
-- NOT normalized: customer_name repeated on every order row
-- (id, customer_name, customer_email, item, price)

-- Normalized: split into two tables
-- customers(id, name, email)
-- orders(id, customer_id, item, price)
commonMistakes: Over-normalizing a reporting/analytics table — sometimes deliberate redundancy (denormalization) is the right call for read-heavy workloads.
lessons.careerRelevance: Interviewers routinely hand you an un-normalized table and ask you to normalize it.

lessons.title: Indexes & how lookups get fast
objectives: Explain why an index speeds up lookups
Know the trade-off indexes carry
Explain how index changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect index with B-tree and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Without an index, finding a row means scanning every row (O(n)) — a full table scan. An index is a separate, sorted structure (usually a B-tree) that lets the database jump straight to matching rows (roughly O(log n)).
commonMistakes: Indexing every column 'just in case' — this bloats storage and slows down writes for indexes that are never used by a query.
lessons.careerRelevance: 'Why is this query slow?' in an interview or on the job is very often answered by 'there's no index here.'

lessons.title: NoSQL vs SQL: when to use which
objectives: Contrast document/key-value/relational models
Pick the right store for a given access pattern
Explain how document store changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect document store with key-value store and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: SQL databases enforce a fixed schema and strong relational integrity — great when your data has clear structure and relationships (orders, customers, inventory). NoSQL stores relax this: document stores (MongoDB) hold flexible JSON-like records; key-value stores (Redis, DynamoDB) trade query flexibility for extreme speed at massive scale.
examples:
# SQL: 'give me all orders over $50 for customers in Dubai, joined with product names'
# -> relational, needs joins and constraints -> SQL

# Key-value: 'get this user's session by session_id, sub-millisecond'
# -> no relationships, pure lookup speed -> Redis/DynamoDB
commonMistakes: Choosing NoSQL purely because it's trendy, then rebuilding joins and constraints in application code — usually a sign SQL was the right choice.
lessons.careerRelevance: System design interviews frequently ask you to justify SQL vs NoSQL for a given service.

lessons.title: PostgreSQL in practice
objectives: Write a PostgreSQL-specific CREATE TABLE and INSERT using Postgres conventions
Explain how PostgreSQL changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect PostgreSQL with SERIAL and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: PostgreSQL is a specific, widely-used SQL database -- everything you've learned about schemas, keys, and normalization applies directly. Postgres adds practical tools on top: SERIAL/IDENTITY columns for auto-incrementing ids, RETURNING to get a row back from an INSERT in one round trip, and rich data types like JSONB and arrays that go beyond standard SQL.
commonMistakes: Forgetting UNIQUE or NOT NULL constraints and only discovering the gap once duplicate or missing data has already been written in production.
lessons.careerRelevance: PostgreSQL is the most commonly used relational database in real backend jobs -- naming it specifically (not just 'SQL') is what most job postings actually ask for.

lessons.title: Transactions & ACID Properties
objectives: Explain why transactions exist and use commit/rollback to keep multi-step operations consistent
Explain how transaction changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect transaction with ACID and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A transaction groups multiple database operations into one all-or-nothing unit -- either every operation in it succeeds and is committed, or if anything fails partway through, the whole thing rolls back as if none of it happened.
commonMistakes: Performing a multi-step operation (like a funds transfer) as separate, un-transacted writes -- if anything fails between the steps, the database is left in a genuinely inconsistent state.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding when an operation needs to be wrapped in a transaction -- and being able to explain why -- is one of the most common practical database judgment calls in real backend work, and a frequent interview topic.
lessons.explain: A transaction groups multiple database operations into one all-or-nothing unit -- either every operation in it succeeds and is committed, or if anything fails partway through, the whole thing rolls back as if none of it happened.

lessons.title: Transaction isolation levels & anomalies
objectives: Explain dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms, and what isolation levels trade off
Explain how Read Committed changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Read Committed with Repeatable Read and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Isolation controls how concurrent transactions can observe one another. Weak isolation improves concurrency but can expose anomalies; stronger isolation reduces anomalies at the cost of more coordination or retries.
lessons.example: Two transfers read the same balance of 100. If both independently decide that withdrawing 80 is allowed, a weakly coordinated implementation can overspend. A transaction must protect the invariant with appropriate locking, serializable behavior, or a conditional atomic update.
commonMistakes: Assuming ACID means every transaction automatically behaves as if it ran alone.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in modern software/backend internship requirements or technical interviews and strengthens transferable engineering fundamentals.

lessons.title: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking
objectives: Choose between optimistic version checks and pessimistic row locks for concurrent updates
Explain how SELECT FOR UPDATE changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect SELECT FOR UPDATE with optimistic locking and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Pessimistic locking reserves rows before changing them, which is useful when conflicts are likely but can block other work. Optimistic locking lets work proceed and rejects an update if a version changed, which is useful when conflicts are rare.
lessons.example: Pessimistic pattern: BEGIN; SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN (...) FOR UPDATE; validate both rows; UPDATE accounts ...; COMMIT. Optimistic pattern: UPDATE accounts SET balance=?, version=version+1 WHERE id=? AND version=?; verify exactly one row changed.
commonMistakes: Locking the same pair of rows in different orders in different code paths.

lessons.title: Query plans, EXPLAIN & index trade-offs
objectives: Read the main idea of an execution plan and decide when an index can help
Explain how EXPLAIN changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect EXPLAIN with sequential scan and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: A database optimizer chooses a plan based on estimated cost. EXPLAIN shows operations such as scans, joins, and sorts so you can investigate slow queries instead of guessing.
lessons.example:
EXPLAIN SELECT id, balance FROM accounts WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

A useful candidate index might begin with user_id and then created_at, but the correct choice depends on real data distribution and workload.

lessons.title: Redis caching & database consistency
objectives: Explain cache-aside and reason about stale-cache windows during database writes
Explain how Redis changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Redis with cache-aside and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Redis is often used as an in-memory cache because reads are fast and data structures are convenient. In cache-aside, the application reads the cache first, falls back to the database on a miss, then populates the cache.
lessons.example:
Read: cache GET key -> on miss read DB -> SET key with TTL.
Write: commit DB transaction first -> invalidate cache key.
If invalidation fails, retry it and keep TTL finite so stale data cannot live forever.
commonMistakes: Updating the cache first and then treating the database write as guaranteed.

lessons.title: B+ trees & LSM trees: how storage indexes work
objectives: Compare B+ tree and LSM-tree trade-offs for reads, writes, and storage layout
Explain how B+ tree changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect B+ tree with LSM tree and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: B+ trees keep sorted keys in page-friendly tree nodes and are widely used for database indexes because they support point lookups and ordered range scans. LSM trees buffer writes and later merge sorted files through compaction, trading faster sequential writes for more complicated reads and background work.
lessons.example: B+ tree intuition: follow a small number of page pointers to a sorted leaf, then scan neighboring leaves for a range. LSM intuition: write to memory/log first, flush sorted runs, and compact runs in the background.

lessons.title: MySQL & PostgreSQL production fundamentals
objectives: Recognize shared relational concepts and practical differences between common production SQL databases
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: backup and restore, replication, read replicas, partitioning / sharding.
Explain how MySQL changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect MySQL with PostgreSQL and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: MySQL and PostgreSQL are both production relational databases with transactions, indexes, constraints, and SQL, but they differ in features and operational details. The transferable skill is relational reasoning: model constraints in the database, parameterize queries, use transactions deliberately, keep connection pools bounded, and inspect query plans.
lessons.example: Production checklist: use parameterized queries; enforce important uniqueness/foreign-key constraints in the database; keep transactions short; use a connection pool; measure slow queries before tuning.
commonMistakes: Treating database choice as a reason to relearn SQL from zero.

lessons.title: Schema migrations & safe database changes
objectives: Plan backward-compatible schema changes that can be deployed without breaking live services
Explain how migration changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect migration with backward compatibility and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: A production schema change is a deployment problem, not just an ALTER TABLE statement. A safe pattern is expand-contract: first add a compatible new field/table, deploy code that can handle both old and new shapes, backfill data, switch reads/writes, then remove the old structure later.
lessons.example: Rename safely: add new column -> dual-write or backfill -> deploy readers using new column -> verify -> stop old writes -> remove old column in a later release.
commonMistakes: Renaming or deleting a field in the same deployment that updates application code.

exercises.title: SQL vs NoSQL call
exercises.prompt: A service needs sub-millisecond lookups of a shopping cart by session_id, no relationships, no reporting needs. SQL or NoSQL — justify it.
exercises.hint: key-value store; access pattern has no relational need

exercises.title: Diagnose a lost-transfer bug
exercises.prompt: A funds-transfer feature runs two separate, un-transacted UPDATE statements: debit account A, then credit account B. During a load test, a server crash between the two statements causes account A to be debited with account B never credited. What's the actual fix, and why doesn't 'just add a try/catch' solve it?
exercises.hint: wrap both UPDATEs in a single database transaction (BEGIN...COMMIT) -- a try/catch in the application only handles errors the app can see; it can't undo a write the database already committed, or recover from the process crashing entirely between the two statements

exercises.title: Diagnose a slow query with the wrong index
exercises.prompt: A `users` table has an index on `signup_date`, but the actual slow query filters by `email`, which has no index and triggers a full table scan on a million-row table. What's the mismatch here, and what should change?
exercises.hint: the index exists on a column that isn't actually queried -- indexes only speed up lookups on the columns they cover, so an index needs to match the real query pattern (email, here), not just any column that seemed important when the schema was designed

interviewPreparation.q: Why do you need a database transaction for something like a funds transfer, instead of just two separate UPDATE statements?
interviewPreparation.a: Without a transaction, a crash or error between the two writes leaves the database in a genuinely inconsistent state -- money debited from one account with no corresponding credit -- and there's no way to know from the outside which steps actually completed. A transaction's atomicity guarantees both writes happen or neither does.

interviewPreparation.q: What does the 'I' in ACID (isolation) actually protect against?
interviewPreparation.a: Race conditions between concurrent transactions -- without isolation, two transactions reading and writing the same row can interleave in ways where each looks correct on its own, but the combined result is wrong (e.g. two withdrawals both reading the same starting balance before either commits, overdrawing an account that should have been prevented).

interviewPreparation.q: How would you decide which columns to index on a large table?
interviewPreparation.a: Look at the actual query patterns hitting that table -- which columns appear in WHERE clauses, JOINs, or ORDER BY on the queries that are actually slow -- rather than indexing preemptively. An index on a rarely-queried column adds write overhead for no real benefit, while a genuinely hot query without the right index causes full table scans.

interviewPreparation.q: When would you choose NoSQL over a relational database for a given use case?
interviewPreparation.a: When the access pattern is simple key-based lookups with no need for joins or complex reporting, and schema flexibility matters more than strict consistency guarantees -- a session store or a shopping cart by session ID is a common example. For anything needing multi-table relationships, transactions across multiple records, or ad-hoc reporting, relational usually wins.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you diagnose a slow-running query in production?
interviewPreparation.a: Check whether it's actually using an index (via the database's query plan/EXPLAIN output) or falling back to a full table scan, and confirm the index that exists actually matches the columns the query filters or joins on -- a common real-world surprise is an index existing on the 'wrong' column relative to what's actually slow.

capstone.title: Design, index, and transact against a real data layer
capstone.description: Take the backend service and API you've already built (or a new one) and give it a real, production-minded data layer: a normalized schema with correct keys and constraints, indexes chosen from actual query patterns rather than guesswork, and at least one multi-step operation correctly wrapped in a transaction so it can't leave data in a half-finished state. This capstone is about the data layer specifically -- the discipline that makes a backend trustworthy under real, concurrent load, not just correct in a single-user demo.
deliverables: A normalized schema (justify your normal form choices) with correct primary/foreign keys and constraints
At least one index added specifically because of a real, stated query pattern -- not a guess -- with a before/after note on what it improved
At least one multi-step operation (e.g. a transfer, an order-plus-inventory-decrement) correctly wrapped in a transaction, with a written explanation of what would go wrong without it
A short note on one deliberate SQL vs NoSQL (or table design) trade-off you made and why
capstone.portfolioTips: The transaction requirement is the detail that separates 'I can write SQL' from 'I understand data integrity under real, concurrent, occasionally-failing conditions' -- make sure your written explanation of the failure mode you're preventing is concrete, not just a definition of ACID.

industryUsage.usage: Relies heavily on database transactions for payment processing, where a partially-completed money movement is not an acceptable failure mode under any circumstance.
Uses careful indexing and query-pattern-driven schema design at massive scale, where an unindexed query on a huge table can measurably affect real infrastructure cost and latency.
As a fintech, transaction correctness (ACID guarantees around account balances and transfers) is a first-order engineering requirement, not an optional nicety.
